angle: A commander whose power is not a stat but an access counter — and the issue that put ten combo lines through the checker, cleared exactly one, discovered that the one it cleared was only half of what everybody says it is, and turned the other half into the best arithmetic on the page.

The ladder: 3, 10, 23, 28, 33 — and why the fifth colour buys you nothing
26 cards your commander can never find, including every counterspell in the deck
The loop's life cost is 0, not 2 — and the two lands you should never tap

departments.headline: COUNT COLOURS, NOT CARDS
departments.dek: Why do good Sisay pilots pass with five untapped lands and no activation? Because the number that decides what she can find is not printed on her card — it is the count of distinct colours sitting next to her.

callouts.title: LAND HER, THEN WAIT
callouts.text: Sisay costs {2}{W} and the model puts her on the battlefield on turn three in 8,028 of 10,000 seeded games — mean 2.96, 99.1% by turn six. She is a 2/2 the turn she arrives and her gate reads 'mana value less than 2', which is three cards in the entire deck. Casting her is never the hard part. Nothing about this turn is supposed to look dangerous.

callouts.title: BUY THE SECOND COLOUR
callouts.text: Every colour among your OTHER legendary permanents is +1/+1 on her and one more rung on the gate. Katilda, Kinnan, Lotho, Saffi, Kutzil and Kambal each buy two rungs for two or three mana on a body nobody wants to remove. Derevi buys three on one card.

callouts.title: THE 2-TO-3 STEP IS THE GAME
callouts.text: The ladder runs 3, 10, 23, 28, 33 legal targets at power 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Going from two colours to three adds thirteen targets — the largest jump in the deck, and the moment a pile of undersized legends becomes a toolbox that answers almost anything.

callouts.title: STOP CLIMBING AT FOUR
callouts.text: Nothing in this list costs more than five, so four distinct colours already unlocks all 33. The fifth colour buys combat stats and Jodah's anthem and precisely zero new access. Chasing it is the most common way to spend a turn on nothing.

callouts.title: PAY THE BILL, NOT THE MANA COUNT
callouts.text: {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} is five coloured pips with zero generic. Six cards in the deck can produce several of them at once — Bloom Tender, Faeburrow Elder, Jegantha, Esika, Relic of Legends and Selvala — and the goldfish assembles Sisay alongside one of them 55.8% of the time by turn six. Count coloured sources, never total mana.

captions.Sisay, Weatherlight Captain: **THE ACCESS COUNTER:** +1/+1 for each colour among your other legendary permanents, and a gate of 'mana value less than her power.' Her stat line is a scoreboard for how much of your library is legal.
captions.Derevi, Empyrial Tactician: **THREE RUNGS, ONE CARD:** green, white and blue at mana value 3 takes Sisay from 2/2 to 5/5 and the fetch pool from 3 cards to 28. Nothing else in the deck does that in a single play.
captions.Bloom Tender: **THE FUEL SHE CANNOT FIND:** it taps for one mana of each colour among your permanents — scaling on the exact resource the ladder scales on — and it is not legendary, so she can never go and get it.

pilot_tips.text: Take Mox Amber for the mana, never for the rung — it is colourless, so it is the one fetch that widens nothing.
Land a two-colour legend before you ever pay the five pips; activating into an empty board spends WUBRG on a three-card pool.

departments.pull_quote: Her power is not a stat. It is how much of your library you are allowed to touch.
departments.note: Hero image is Sisay's art_crop; the callout ladder is the spread's real entry point and should be able to be read on its own by someone who never reads the body copy. Body copy comes from manual_prose.how_it_wins — do not restate it in the furniture.

departments.headline: THE ONE CARD THAT FINDS THE OTHER THIRTY-THREE
departments.dek: Your commander is the only card the format guarantees you — and in this deck she is also the only card that reaches the rest of the deck. So what does Commander charge you for that, and what does it quietly hand you for free?
departments.body:
Start with the rule that makes this a different game. CR 903.6: "At the start of the game, each player puts their commander from their deck face up into the command zone." Sisay, Weatherlight Captain is not a card you hope to draw — she is face up on the table before anybody has looked at seven cards, and in a deck built on thirty-three one-of legendary permanents that guarantee is the whole architecture. Singleton is why: CR 903.5b requires every nonbasic card in the 99 to have a different English name, so consistency in this format normally comes from redundancy of effect rather than copies of a card. This deck buys consistency a different way. It runs one repeatable battlefield tutor and treats thirty-three singletons as a sideboard it can reach into, and the tutor is the one card the format promises you every single game. That is why Keep or Ship, four departments from now, asks your opening hand for colours and fuel and never once asks it for a payoff.

Now the bill, and read the ladder beside this file while you do. CR 903.8: a commander cast from the command zone "costs an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game." Sisay is {2}{W}, so the schedule is three mana, then five, then seven, then nine. Put those against the simulation's own numbers: 4.06 mean available mana on turn four, 5.87 on turn six, 8.27 on turn ten. The first cast is trivially on curve — the model has her down by turn three in 8,028 of 10,000 games. The second cast is a five-mana turn that leaves you roughly one mana, which in this deck means a turn with no activation in it. The third is the entire turn and most of the next one.

Here is the distinction good pilots make and bad ones don't. Spot removal aimed at Sisay costs you the tax and the tempo — it does not cost you the ladder, because her power comes from colours among your other legendary permanents and those are still standing when she comes back. A sweeper is the expensive one: it takes the rungs, and Sisay returns to a battlefield where her gate reads "mana value less than 2" and three cards in the deck qualify. Price those two threats differently. Against a pod that answers creatures one at a time, pay the tax and rebuild. Against a pod holding a wrath, keep a two-colour legend in hand rather than on the battlefield, because the hand copy restores two rungs after the wipe and the board copy dies with everything else.

So: protection or speed? The strategy companion is honest about the trade — protection slots and held mana cost you every game, while removal only costs you some — and Cullen's taxonomy splits the options into constant protection, single-use instants, and flexible modal slots. This deck's version of that argument has an unusual shape, because most of its insurance is unfetchable. The simulation has protection available in 88.4% of games and 79.8% by turn six, at a mean of turn 2.3 — but Fierce Guardianship, Flawless Maneuver, Heroic Intervention, Grand Abolisher, Silence and all six counterspells are non-legendary, which means Sisay cannot go and get a single one of them. Exactly four insurance pieces sit inside her range: Shalai, Voice of Plenty, Flowering of the White Tree, Dihada, Binder of Wills, and Plaza of Heroes in the mana base. Our rule: fetch Shalai on the activation before you need her, because she gives hexproof to you and to every other creature you control and cannot protect herself.

Color identity, and the joke this deck is built on. CR 903.4 defines color identity as "the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card's mana cost or rules text," and Sisay's rules text carries {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}. Her identity is therefore all five colours and the 99 is unrestricted — nothing in Magic is locked out of this deck. Then the same five symbols that opened the door become the door's price: her activation is five coloured pips with zero generic, paid over and over. Color identity gives you every card in the format and the activation cost takes most of your mana base back. That is why three of this deck's own accelerants cannot pay her at all — Sol Ring makes {C}{C} against a cost with no generic component, Delighted Halfling's coloured mana is restricted to legendary spells and an activated ability is not a spell, and Unclaimed Territory is creature-spells-only. It is also why Command Tower here is genuinely any colour, and why Plaza of Heroes' third mode, "add one mana of any color among legendary permanents you control," is one of the best lines of text in the deck.

Is the 21-damage clock real? CR 903.10a: "A player who's been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game." Sisay at three colours is a 5/5, which is five connections; at four colours she is a 6/6, which is four. That is a shorter clock than you would guess and it is still not a plan — you need her untapped to activate, and her ability has no tap symbol precisely so you can do both, which is a bigger deal than the damage. Track the number on one opponent as a tiebreaker, and note the one card that turns her connections into value on purpose: Kutzil, Malamet Exemplar draws you a card whenever a creature with power greater than its base power connects, and a pumped Sisay is always that creature.

The political read is the gentlest thing about this deck and the most useful. A freshly cast Sisay is harmless and experienced players know it — a 2/2 with a gate of "mana value less than 2" is not worth a removal spell. Your grace period ends at the third colour, not at the commander. Sequence the colours onto bodies that read fair, hold the five pips until you intend to spend them, and remember the asymmetry almost nobody else at the table has: your scariest cards live in your library and you can reach them at will, so you never need to hold a finisher in hand. ★ One open question, flagged rather than stamped: whether Sisay may activate on the turn she lands. Her cost contains no tap symbol, which on a plain reading of the summoning-sickness rule means yes — but the case file we wrote to prove it did not clear our checker inside the iteration bound, so it appears in this issue as judgment and not as a verdict. Judge's Desk names it.

captions.Plaza of Heroes: **READ THE THIRD MODE:** 'any color among legendary permanents you control' is unrestricted mana her activation can spend. The legendary-spell mode above it never can — and the exile mode is one of only four insurance pieces she can fetch.

pilot_tips.text: Cast Sol Ring for the commander and never count it toward the activation — {C}{C} pays zero of a five-pip cost with no generic component.
Fetch Shalai one activation before you need her: she gives hexproof to you and every other creature you control, and never to herself.

departments.pull_quote: Colour identity hands you every card in the format, then the activation cost takes your mana base back.
departments.note: Mandatory Commander Mandate department. CR 903.6, 903.5b, 903.8, 903.4 and 903.10a are quoted verbatim in the body and carry ✓. The final paragraph's summoning-sickness note is explicitly ★ and must render in coaching costume — stack 001 failed the iteration bound and this issue does not stamp it. The tax ladder table (3 / 5 / 7 / 9) is renderer-generated from cmc 3; the body reads it against the goldfish mana curve, so keep them on the same spread.

departments.headline: 5.87 MANA, FIVE DIFFERENT COLOURS
departments.dek: Your commander is never the problem — she lands on turn three in 8,028 of 10,000 seeded games. The problem is the mana you actually have on turn six and the five distinct pips you owe every time you want to do something with her.

captions.Faeburrow Elder: **WHY A BODY, NOT A ROCK:** at turn six the model gives you 5.87 mana on average. Paying five different colours out of that is only possible if one permanent covers several pips at once.

pilot_tips.text: Treat Bloom Tender as the difference between casting Sisay and using her — the five-colour target assembles at a mean of turn 4.22 and only 55.8% of the time by turn six.

departments.pull_quote: The model never struggles to cast her. It struggles to pay her.
departments.note: Meters, the turn table and the stated-assumptions box are renderer-generated from goldfish_metrics.json — seed 42, 10,000 iterations. Cite figures exactly: mean cast turn 2.963, median 3, 99.1% by turn six; keep-first-seven 84.2%; mean mulligans 0.183; mean available mana 4.063 at turn four and 5.869 at turn six; land-drop hit rate 0.842 at four, 0.735 at five, 0.637 at six. The four target meters are the departmental payoff and should sit above the turn table: five-colour source 67.9%, three-colour legend 52.5%, early accelerant 74.7%, protection 88.4%. This is a dense analysis spread and the pull quote is its exit ramp into The Kill — keep it at the foot of the page.

departments.headline: HALF AN INFINITE
departments.dek: The combo data calls Najeela plus Derevi a two-card infinite and uses it to set this deck's bracket floor. We resolved it against the rules, re-audited it three times, and the verdict came back partially accurate — which is worth more to you at the table than a yes would have been.

callouts.title: COMBAT ONE IS ON YOUR LANDS
callouts.text: You declare Najeela and Derevi. Exactly one Warrior is declared, so exactly one trigger and one token — and a token put onto the battlefield attacking never 'attacked', so it does not chain inside the combat that made it. Three attackers, six damage, three Derevi untap triggers against a five-mana activation. Combat one is funded by the lands you had untapped before combat, not by the loop.

callouts.title: COMBAT TWO BREAKS EVEN
callouts.text: The activation untapped the attackers and gave them haste, so the token can be declared again: three declared, two of them Warriors, two new tokens, five attackers, five Derevi triggers. Five triggers against a fixed five-mana cost is exact break-even. The mechanism is a cycle inside one damage step — tap a land, pass priority, let one trigger resolve and untap it, tap it again.

callouts.title: COMBAT THREE RUNS AWAY
callouts.text: Nine attackers, nine triggers, cost still five. Attackers follow A' = 2A − 1: 3, 5, 9, 17, 33. Derevi's triggers equal the attacker count while Najeela's bill never moves, so the margin only widens from here.

callouts.title: COUNT THE DAMAGE, NOT THE COMBATS
callouts.text: Damage per combat is A + 3: six, eight, twelve, twenty. Cumulative on the first defending player: 6, 14, 26, 46. They are at −6 during combat four's damage step and lose as a state-based action before anybody gets priority.

callouts.title: THE ARMY DOES NOT DISBAND
callouts.text: The list of ways a creature is removed from combat is exhaustive, and 'the player they were attacking has left the game' is not on it. The seventeen creatures still attacking a dead player stay in combat, so that combat's activation still untaps them — and because every opponent is already a defending player, combat five redeclares all seventeen at the next seat. Thirty-three attackers, thirty-six damage. Combat six ends it.

callouts.title: THE BILL IS ZERO LIFE
callouts.text: Command Tower covers {B} through Sisay's five-colour identity and Plaza of Heroes' third mode covers W, U, R and G off the colours Najeela and Derevi already put on the board — five taps needing only three Plaza untaps, which is exactly what combat one's three triggers supply. City of Brass and Mana Confluence never have to be tapped, because activating a mana ability is never mandatory. The two life per combat you will see quoted is the naive line's price, not a floor.

captions.Najeela, the Blade-Blossom: **THE ENGINE, AND THE BILL:** untap all attacking creatures, trample, lifelink, haste, one more combat — for {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}, every single time. The cost is the reason this is not a two-card combo.
captions.Derevi, Empyrial Tactician: **THE REFUND:** one untap trigger per creature that connects, not one per damage event. Three in combat one, five in combat two, nine in combat three — that curve is the whole loop.
captions.Plaza of Heroes: **THE LAND THAT DOES THE WORK:** the third mode covers W, U, R and G off Najeela and Derevi alone, and it is the land Derevi's triggers untap three times.

pilot_tips.text: Never start the loop expecting combat one to refund itself — three triggers against a five-mana cost means your untapped lands pay for the first activation.
Leave City of Brass and Mana Confluence untapped for the whole loop; the five pips come from Command Tower and Plaza of Heroes and the life cost is zero.

departments.pull_quote: Three, five, nine, seventeen, thirty-three — and the cost never moves off five.
departments.note: This is the issue's peak and it carries exactly one case, so the ambition has to come from the arithmetic rather than from volume. Give callouts 1–3 the widest treatment on the spread — the break-even point is the single most transferable idea in the issue. The correction is the feature, not a footnote: the headline, the dek and the pull quote all say the same honest thing three ways. Renderer pulls the intro prose from manual_prose.combo_lines['002'] and the result line from the stack's final_state summary; the dossier pointer goes to Case A-002. Do not let any furniture here refer to the Faeburrow Elder, Esika or Selvala variants as verified — they are not.

departments.headline: NOBODY KILLS A 2/2
departments.dek: You resolve on turn three in 8,028 of 10,000 simulated games and the table lets you — because a fresh Sisay genuinely is harmless. Here is the exact board state where that stops being true, and the removal that actually beats you when it does.

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW: FIVE OPEN COLOURS
callouts.text: Five untapped colour-producing sources next to an untapped Sisay is the board state that flips you. Anyone counting mana reads it as 'activation available' — and her ability has no tap symbol, so 'she only just came down' is not the reprieve opponents assume it is.

callouts.title: THE LOUDER TELL IS THE BATTERY
callouts.text: An omni-mana body resolving — Bloom Tender, Faeburrow Elder, Jegantha, Esika — says more than any legend you fetch. The table knows the activation is five distinct pips with zero generic, so the card that solves that problem is the card that names your turn.

callouts.title: NAJEELA IS THE ANNOUNCEMENT
callouts.text: Fetching Najeela at a bracket 4 pod is read as 'they have it', full stop. Your advantage is that she lives in your library and you can reach her at will, so there is no reason to take her before the turn the mana doubles.

callouts.title: HOW THEY ACTUALLY KILL YOU
callouts.text: Good opponents do not answer Sisay. They answer the rung — the single legend that is your only source of a colour — in response to the activation, so the fetch shrinks. Audit that every turn: which colour is single-sourced? That permanent is the removal magnet.

captions.Shalai, Voice of Plenty: **THE RETIREMENT PLAN:** hexproof for you and every other creature you control ends the shrink-the-ladder attack permanently. One fetch, one whole category of interaction blanked.
captions.Rhystic Study: **THE TELL YOU DIDN'T CHOOSE:** a Game Changer, non-legendary, and the fastest way to become the archenemy without advancing your engine one rung.

pilot_tips.text: Hold Rhystic Study at a table still deciding who to hit — it makes you the archenemy and moves your ladder not at all.
Use Loran's draw-with-an-opponent mode as spotlight management; it is the only political card in the deck that arrives attached to a body you wanted anyway.

departments.pull_quote: They do not kill your commander. They kill the one legend that is your only green.
departments.note: Deliberate breather after the peak: reflection mode, no new mechanics, callouts and prose only. Body copy is manual_prose.threat_assessment, which already carries the four tells and the mirror — the callouts are the scannable version of it and must not contradict it. Callout 1 is the THREAT WINDOW component required by STYLEv3 §5.1.

departments.headline: TWO ACTIVATIONS, TWO WRONG ANSWERS
departments.dek: Both of these turns hand you a card that is obviously the strongest thing you can fetch, and in both of them we take something else. Commit out loud before you read the branches.

captions.Kutzil, Malamet Exemplar: **THE HATEBEAR NOBODY PRICES:** 'Your opponents can't cast spells during your turn' — a 3/3 Cat that turns every future activation into a window they are not allowed to answer.

pilot_tips.text: Announce the activation before you decide the fetch — her ability names no target and her power is read once, on resolution, so the greedy attempt is free.

departments.pull_quote: Fetch the enabler. Keep the tell in the library.
departments.note: Two validated decision spreads, rendered in artifact order: 001 activating-into-open-mana, then 002 the-scary-fetch-and-the-correct-fetch. Headline and dek must not name Shalai or Kutzil — the reader has to commit first. The stale 'no checker-passed resolution' sentences in both artifacts were corrected before render once stack 002 cleared.

departments.headline: THE SHAPE THAT HATES YOU
departments.dek: One of these four archetypes attacks a five-pip, zero-generic, repeatable activation more directly than it attacks anything else in the format. Name it before you look at the meters.

threats.read: This is the one. Five coloured pips with zero generic, activated repeatedly, is the most tax-exposed engine shape in Commander — there is no generic component to pay around, so anything raising the cost of turning mana into effects, or keeping lands tapped, hits you harder than it hits a ramp deck. You are the beatdown here and the role is forced: race the lock's completion, because you do not own the long game underneath one. Recount your activations under the tax rather than your cards, and recount honestly — three of your own accelerants cannot pay a single pip.

Your posture inverts completely: hold the pips for interaction and count the table's open mana instead of advancing the ladder, because a ladder is worth nothing if the game ends before it matures. The structural problem is that your interaction is exactly the part Sisay cannot reach — all six counterspells, both free protection instants, Grand Abolisher and Drannith Magistrate are non-legendary. Two fetchable pieces do real work and you should reach for them before you reach for a finisher.

Assume the wrath — across four players one is near-certain — and price it double, because it takes the board and drops the ladder from 28 targets back to three, with no legendary lands to give you a mana-value-0 floor. The Sisay-specific reading of 'commit only as much as wins' is about where the colour lives, not how much you show: keep a two-colour legend in hand, because a hand copy restores two rungs and a board copy dies with everything else. Your indestructible instants beat destruction and do nothing against exile or −X/−X.

Roughly 120 life behind three defences means you never race, and you are not being asked to — your answers here are virtual rather than spent. One fetch blanks plans from three seats at once, which is the only economical way to answer aggression in a four-player game, and every piece that does it is a legendary permanent at mana value 2 to 4 sitting inside the pool from two colours onward. If you get pulled into a two-player race, treat it as a subgame, spend the minimum that wins it, and keep watching the other seats.

captions.Toxic Deluge: **THE WIPE YOU TIME:** priced in life so it scales to any board, and you are the deck that rebuilds cheapest — provided you kept a colour-diverse legend in hand instead of committing it.
captions.Teferi, Time Raveler: **TWO MATCHUPS, ONE CARD:** sorcery-speed-only deletes instant-speed combo and instant-speed answers to your activation in the same line of text.

pilot_tips.text: Against stax, fetch Loran for the piece that breaks the lock on you — not for the scariest permanent on the table.

departments.pull_quote: You do not run removal. You fetch reasons your opponents cannot use theirs.
departments.note: Four threat boxes in threat order, most dangerous first — the dek asks the reader to guess and the ordering is the answer. Fair-value midrange is the fifth matchup and the one you are favoured in; it lives in the prose from manual_prose.matchups rather than in a box, so the boxes stay a scouting report on danger. Every named out is verified present in the 99.

departments.headline: THE HALF SHE CAN SEE
departments.dek: The most useful way to sort ninety-nine cards here is not by colour or by curve — it is by whether your commander can go and get them. Twenty-six of these she never will.

roster.role: The ladder — colours on cheap bodies
cards: Rona, Herald of Invasion // Rona, Tolarian Obliterator

roster.role: The pip battery — the only six cards that can pay her
cards: Esika, God of the Tree // The Prismatic Bridge

roster.role: The tax shell — this deck's removal suite
Insurance and answers she can fetch
The kill, and the cards that untap it
The four Game Changers — and she can see none of them
Acceleration — and what it cannot buy

departments.note: Groups are ranked, not alphabetical: the ladder and the battery lead because they are what the issue is about, and the Game Changers get their own four-card group because they are simultaneously the bracket floor and the clearest illustration of the deck's blind spot. The remaining 36 lands fall into the renderer's Depth bucket, which is correct — manual_prose.card_roles carries a real teaching line for every one of them, including which pip each fetch land is for. Tiles here deliberately carry no printing credits; the physical cards are Featured Artist's subject one page later. Note for the renderer: synergy_graph.json has no entry for Sisay and no in-deck partners for Najeela, Emiel, Relic of Legends or Jodah, so role chips will be sparse on exactly the deck's most load-bearing tiles — that is a data gap, not a design choice.

departments.headline: EIGHTY-ONE HANDS, NINETY-NINE CARDS
departments.dek: The busiest artist in this deck painted five cards. The second busiest painted four, and they are all the same land cycle. So what does a deck look like when nobody was collecting anything?

featured.note:
There is no featured artist here in the usual sense, and pretending otherwise would be the kind of small lie this magazine exists to avoid. Eighty-one artists painted the ninety-nine cards counted in this deck, across sixty-six different sets. The leader is Steven Belledin with five cards — five percent of the list — and second place is four.

That number is the story. A five-colour singleton toolbox is the most artistically dispersed thing you can build in Commander: thirty-nine lands drawn from every fixing cycle printed in twenty years, thirty-four legendary permanents pulled one at a time out of whichever set happened to print a two-colour body at mana value two. Nobody bought a box that landed on this deck. It was assembled one card at a time by somebody counting colours, and the art follows the counting.

Belledin's five are worth a look precisely because we are not going to claim they mean anything. Exotic Orchard, Forest, Loran of the Third Path, Mikaeus, the Lunarch and Mox Amber — and three of those five are load-bearing in ways this issue has already explained. Mox Amber and Mikaeus are two of the three cards a cold-start Sisay can legally find at power 2, and Loran is the only artifact and enchantment answer in the deck stapled to a legendary body, which makes it the only one she can fetch. One artist happens to sit on the bottom rung of the ladder and on the deck's single tutorable answer. That is a coincidence, and coincidences are more fun when you say so.

One counting note, because it is the whole reason this department is honest. Ninety-nine cards, one hundred copies: the only card in the deck with a quantity above one is a basic Plains. Nils Hamm painted Bloom Tender and that Plains, which is two cards and three copies — and we count him as a two. Per card, never per copy. In a deck like this one the difference is a single basic land; in a deck with twenty-two of them it is the difference between a fact and a flattering lie.

also_worth_noting.note: Four cards, and all four are shocklands — Hallowed Fountain, Overgrown Tomb, Steam Vents, Temple Garden. This is concentration with a structural cause rather than a curatorial one: one artist covered a chunk of the cycle, and the pilot bought the lands the mana base needed. Nobody chose a painter here; four different colour pairs did.

Flooded Strand and Windswept Heath — two of the eight fetch lands, and a neat illustration of why this deck is dispersed. Eight fetches, five duals, eight pain and pod lands and five basics were bought for the pips they produce, and the signatures arrived as a side effect of the colour requirement.

Esper Sentinel and Grand Abolisher: two non-legendary tax pieces, both excellent, both permanently outside Sisay's reach. If you want a single image of this deck's blind spot, it is these two cards sitting next to each other in the gallery and nowhere in the fetch pool.
Jegantha, the Wellspring and Sheoldred, the Apocalypse — the deck's single-tap five-colour source and its scarcest colour's best body, sharing nothing except a hand.

captions.Mox Amber: **THE BOTTOM RUNG:** the only mana-value-0 permanent Sisay can find, and the cheapest fetch in the deck. Steven Belledin, and one of the five.
captions.Loran of the Third Path: **THE ONLY FETCHABLE ANSWER:** the deck's sole artifact and enchantment removal on a legendary body — which is what puts it inside the tutor's range at all.
captions.Plains: **ONE CARD, TWO COPIES:** the only card in the deck with a quantity above one, and the reason this department counts entries rather than copies.

pilot_tips.text: When somebody tells you an artist painted a third of a deck, ask whether they counted cards or copies — in this list, one basic art is the entire difference.

departments.pull_quote: Eighty-one artists, sixty-six sets, and a top score of five. That is not a collection. That is a colour requirement.
departments.note: artist-credits reports standout: null and a note instructing a breadth story — this department runs it as designed and must not manufacture a lead artist. The renderer recomputes every figure; the plan supplies only the choice of who to talk about and the prose. Do NOT let any copy imply curation: there are no drop_runs in this deck, and both concentrations (Belledin's five, Paquette's four) are explicitly named as coincidence and as cycle structure respectively. also_worth_noting is restricted to artists the renderer surfaces in clusters[:6] — Paquette, Forssberg, Deschamps and Rahn all render. Nils Hamm sits seventh and would be silently dropped, so his per-entry-versus-per-copy story lives in the featured note, the Plains caption and the PILOT TIP instead.

departments.headline: FOUR SEVENS, ONE QUESTION
departments.dek: The model keeps 84.2% of first sevens on a simple land rule, so the interesting question was never whether to keep — it is whether the hand you kept can ever pay five different pips. Decide on each of these before you read the verdict.

hands.why: Three lands with an unrestricted source, a one-mana any-colour body, a two-colour legend for the second rung, and the battery piece that pays for the activation. Jodah is uncastable for now and it does not matter — he is a payoff, and payoffs are the part you can fetch later.

hands.verdict: KEEP — three rungs on one card
hands.why: Four lands, an unrestricted rock, and Derevi — green, white and blue on one mana-value-3 card takes Sisay to 5/5 and the pool from 3 cards to 28 by herself. Negate is the half of the deck you are happy to draw rather than fetch.

Both accelerants get her out a turn early and neither pays one pip of what she does there — Sol Ring is colourless, Delighted Halfling's mana is for legendary spells and an activated ability is not a spell. Three five-drops behind two lands is a hand of things you were always going to be able to fetch.

hands.verdict: SHIP — answers with nothing to answer for
hands.why: Four pieces of interaction, zero ladder, and Fierce Guardianship needs a commander on the battlefield to be free. Your interaction is the half of the deck you can afford to draw into later; the enablers are the half you cannot.

captions.Delighted Halfling: **THE TRAP IN A KEEP:** genuine acceleration toward casting her, and zero acceleration toward using her. Read the restriction, not the mana symbol.

pilot_tips.text: Count Delighted Halfling as ramp toward Sisay and nothing toward her ability — its mana is restricted to legendary spells.
Treat Derevi in an opening hand as three ladder rungs, not as a 2/3 flier — she is the single best keep-maker in the deck.

departments.pull_quote: Mulligan for enablers, not for payoffs. The payoffs are the part you can go and get.
departments.note: Renderer prints the keep-first-seven meter at 84.2% and then manual_prose.mulligan. The four hands are illustrative constructions, not simulator output — they are legal singleton sevens drawn from this 99, and the reasons cite the goldfish figures the artifact actually reports (84.2% keep rate, 0.183 mean mulligans, early accelerant 63.8% by turn six at mean turn 2.84). Keep the verdicts below the fold of the reader's eye if the layout allows: the drill only works if they call it first.

departments.headline: FORTY-EIGHT SUGGESTIONS, SIX LEGENDARY
departments.dek: The obsolescence index flags nineteen cards in this list and names forty-eight replacements for them. Only six of those are cards Sisay could ever find — so before you buy one, learn the two questions the index cannot ask.

captions.Mox Amber: **THE EMPTY BOTTOM RUNG:** the deck runs 39 lands and zero legendary ones, so this is the entire mana-value-0 tier of the fetch pool. Every legendary land in the format is a one-card fix — and none of them add a colour to her power.

pilot_tips.text: Ignore the index's Sol Ring swap here — Fellwar Stone makes a colour and Sol Ring makes none of the five you owe.
Never cut Bloom Tender for Delighted Halfling on mana value: the Halfling's mana cannot pay an activated ability, and paying the activation is the whole job.
Until somebody resolves whether a fetched Mikaeus arrives with zero counters, plan your cold start around two live targets rather than three.

departments.pull_quote: The index compares mana values. It has never asked whether a card is legendary.
departments.note: Body copy is manual_prose.upgrades, which already audits the index card by card and names the cross-cluster noise. The single most actionable finding — the empty legendary-land tier at mana value 0 — is the caption's job because it is the one suggestion the index cannot generate at all. Parroting the index unaudited is the one thing this department may not do.

departments.headline: ONE CASE OUT OF THREE
departments.dek: Three resolutions went to the adversarial checker this issue and one came back clean, in three passes. Every citation from that case is reproduced here verbatim — and the two that failed are named below, because what we could not prove is part of the record too.
departments.note: Renderer generates this from checker-passed artifacts only, so Case A-002 is the sole dossier and nothing in it may be summarised, truncated or paraphrased. The dek must name the two failures without presenting any of their content: stack 001 (the Sisay tutor chain) and stack 003 (Relic of Legends versus summoning sickness) both exhausted the three-iteration bound and are held as open questions. If the renderer can carry a short standing sidebar under the dossier, it should list those two titles, their verdict ('fail — iteration bound'), and one line each on what remains unresolved — with no rule numbers and no quotes, so there is no chance of a reader mistaking them for findings. This is the department where an issue with one verified line either earns its credibility or loses it, and naming the misses is how it earns it.

Next issue is EDGAR MARKOV per issue.json. Colophon carries rules version June 19, 2026, the decklist sha a4bcbd50…, goldfish seed 42 at 10,000 iterations, and the bracket line: floor 4 (Optimized), forced independently by four Game Changers — worth stating on the way out, because it is the one claim in this issue that survives even if every remaining combo line is refuted.

rhythm_notes: The canonical order alternates correctly on its own — By the Numbers (analysis) into The Kill (narrative), Know Your Enemy (reference) into The 99 (browsing) — so the work this issue needed was at the peak and on the way down from it. The Kill carries exactly one case where Vol. 001 carried five, so its ambition comes from depth rather than volume: six callout steps walking the combat arithmetic, which is the most transferable thing in the issue, plus the correction stated three ways in the headline, the dek and the pull quote. To keep the approach from feeling thin, First Turns front-loads five callouts and By the Numbers exits on a pull quote rather than on a table, so the reader arrives at the peak already holding the ladder and the mana curve. The descent needed the most attention: with only one dossier, Judge's Desk is a short tail, so Upgrade Watch is deliberately over-furnished (three PILOT TIPs, a caption carrying the issue's single most actionable finding, a pull quote) to hold the last browsing stretch. The Politics Table is the designated breather immediately after the peak — reflection mode, callouts and prose only, no new mechanics — before What's Your Play? spikes back on participation. The 99 and Featured Artist form the long exhale, and Featured Artist carries the issue's second honest-negative beat: The Kill refuses to call a famous combo a two-card infinite, and Featured Artist refuses to invent a curator for a deck that plainly did not have one. Putting those at either end of the recovery arc asserts our credibility twice without either reading as an apology.
gaps: HIGHEST VALUE FIX: stack 001 (the Sisay escalating tutor chain) failed only on the iteration bound, with a single residual defect — a class-generalisation slip at step 11 where a −X/−X death case is stated as a class but priced at exactly −6/−6, ignoring that power can go below zero. The checker itself calls it 'one clause'. Everything else in that artifact, including the whole ladder arithmetic and the summoning-sickness answer, was independently verified correct. Resolving it would convert the issue's central teaching claim — that Sisay may activate the turn she lands, and exactly which mana values each power unlocks — from ★ coaching into ✓ verified, and would change First Turns, The Command Zone and What's Your Play? all at once.

Stack 003 (Relic of Legends versus summoning sickness) failed with a genuinely load-bearing defect, not a clerical one: the artifact derives a mana ceiling from the number of tapped sources when the binding cap is the number of Derevi triggers, because a permanent can be re-tapped in the priority window between trigger resolutions. It also never establishes that Esika has printed vigilance on its front face, which its own step 13 argument depends on. This is the single highest-leverage open question in the deck — it decides whether Sisay chains within one turn or across two — and it is worth a fresh resolve run rather than a patch.

Nine of ten combo lines are unverified and the three that would most change the issue are the other Najeela pairs — with Faeburrow Elder, with Esika, God of the Tree // The Prismatic Bridge, and with Selvala, Heart of the Wilds — all claimed as two-card infinites at bracket 3. Case A-002 gives a ready-made test: each one produces mana, so the break-even arithmetic that refuted the 'two-card' claim for Derevi may resolve differently for them. That is a genuinely interesting result either way and would give The Kill a second and third feature.

goldfish_targets.json has no target for the issue's one verified kill. A target of 'Najeela plus Derevi plus five colour sources' would let By the Numbers tell the reader how often the line the cover is selling is actually available — right now the issue can prove the loop works and cannot say how often you get to use it, which is the obvious question a reader will ask.

Featured Artist is running on a partial view of its own data. artist-credits computes treatments.frame_effects (27 of 99 printings carry the legendary frame) and a 66-set dispersion, and the renderer surfaces only the top two sets plus borderless and foil counts. For a deck whose entire subject is legendary permanents, '27 of 99 printings wear the legendary frame' is the best art fact available and is currently unreachable without authored prose. Worth two rows in the Art File.

Strategy DB gaps this issue routed around, in order of how much they were missed: no section on COMBAT-LOOP finishers as a win-condition class (which is precisely what The Kill needed — why break-even matters more than card count, and why extra-combat loops need a live mana base every iteration); no section on RESTRICTED MANA, the accelerants that cannot pay activated-ability costs, which this deck contains three of; no section on TOOLBOX construction or on ACCESS AS A RESOURCE, which is the issue's whole angle and currently rests on computed counts alone; no section on five-colour mana bases, where Karsten's per-pip tables stop being applicable.

synergy_graph.json has no entry for Sisay, Weatherlight Captain and zero in-deck partners for Najeela, Emiel, Relic of Legends and Jodah, so The 99's role chips will be emptiest on exactly the tiles that matter most. Nothing in this plan depends on the synergy graph, but the roster will look under-annotated at the top and fully annotated in the depth, which is backwards.

There is no third decision spread and there is an obvious one: the wrath-response turn. You hold a two-colour legend and a resolved Sisay, the control seat has four open mana, and the choice is whether to commit the rung now for a bigger fetch or keep it in hand as post-wipe insurance. It is the one major strategic tension in the deck that neither existing spread touches, and manual_prose.matchups already grounds it.
